segments.narration: The Air Force planned to detonate a nuke on the Moon. The study started in May 1958, seven months after Sputnik went up.
On paper it was called A Study of Lunar Research Flights. A ten-man team at the Illinois Institute of Technology ran the numbers.
One of them was a graduate student named Carl Sagan, modelling how far the dust cloud would spread. Why would anyone want the Moon to flash?
Morale. A 1.7 kiloton warhead on the shadowed side would throw up dust lit by the Sun, a flash the whole Soviet Union could see.
The Air Force killed it in January 1959, worried fallout would ruin the Moon for science. Reiffel only admitted the thing existed in 2000.

verdicts.claim: Carl Sagan, then a doctoral student, was responsible for the mathematical projection of the dust cloud's expansion around the Moon, which determined whether the blast would be visible from Earth.

verdicts.claim: The plan called for a W25 warhead with a 1.7-kiloton yield detonated on the Moon's shadowed side, so sunlight hitting the dust cloud would make the explosion visible from Earth, and the motive was Cold War morale after Sputnik.

verdicts.claim: Air Force officials cancelled the project in January 1959 because the risks outweighed the benefits, including fallout compromising future lunar research, and Leonard Reiffel revealed its existence publicly in 2000.
